topics.title: Athletics (Jumping): Meaning and Practical Demonstration of Jumping | Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 9 Physical and Health Education
topics.content:
PHYSICAL AND HEALTH EDUCATION (PHE)
PRIMARY 1 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 9
THEME - SPORTS AND GAMES
PREVIOUS LESSON - Athletics: Long-Distance Races, Types of Long-Distance Races, Basic Activities in Long-Distance Races, and Safety Rules | Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 8 Physical and Health Education
TOPIC - ATHLETICS: JUMPING
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Types of Simple Jumps
3. Practical Demonstration of Jumping
4. Importance of Jumping
5. Safety Rules During Jumping Activities
6. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
7. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of jumping.
2. Identify simple types of jumping activities.
3. Demonstrate simple jumping activities.
4. Mention some benefits of jumping.
5. State safety rules to observe during jumping activities.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils can stand, walk, run and move their legs and feet during simple physical activities.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Pictures or charts showing jumping activities
2. Whistle
3. Cones or markers
4. Rope
5. Soft landing mat or suitable soft ground
6. Open playground
METHODS OF TEACHING
The teacher uses observation, demonstration, questioning, identification, imitation, repetition, discussion and simple practical activities.
The teacher begins by asking pupils to bend their knees and gently jump on the spot.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Physical and Health Education textbook for Primary 1
2. Lagos State Scheme of Work for Physical and Health Education
3. Teacher’s lesson guide
4. Other Relevant
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Jumping is one of the activities performed in athletics. It involves moving the body upward or forward by pushing against the ground with the legs and feet.
Jumping is an important physical activity that helps children exercise their bodies and develop body control.
MEANING OF JUMPING
Jumping is the act of pushing the body off the ground with the feet and moving through the air before landing.
For example, when a pupil bends the knees, pushes against the ground and moves upward, the pupil is jumping.
TYPES OF SIMPLE JUMPS
Some simple jumping activities include:
1. Jumping on the spot: Jumping up and landing in the same place.
2. Forward jumping: Jumping from one point to another in front.
3. Side jumping: Jumping from one side to another.
4. Two-foot jumping: Jumping and landing with both feet.
5. Single-foot jumping: Jumping using one foot and landing safely.
PRACTICAL DEMONSTRATION OF JUMPING
The teacher demonstrates the following activities:
1. Stand upright with both feet together.
2. Bend the knees slightly.
3. Swing the arms gently.
4. Push the body upward with the feet.
5. Land softly with the knees slightly bent.
6. Jump forward over a short distance.
7. Jump sideways over a line or rope placed safely on the ground.
8. Stop and rest when instructed.
Pupils practise the activities under the teacher’s supervision.
IMPORTANCE OF JUMPING
Jumping helps pupils to:
1. Exercise the body.
2. Strengthen the legs.
3. Improve balance.
4. Improve body coordination.
5. Develop strong muscles.
6. Keep the body active.
7. Prepare the body for sports and games.
SAFETY RULES DURING JUMPING ACTIVITIES
Pupils should:
1. Listen to the teacher’s instructions.
2. Warm up before jumping.
3. Jump only in a safe and clear area.
4. Keep enough space between one another.
5. Avoid pushing other pupils.
6. Use soft and safe landing areas.
7. Jump over only safe and low objects.
8. Land softly with the knees slightly bent.
9. Stop when the teacher gives the signal.
10. Report pain or injury to the teacher.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
Multiple Choice Questions
1. Jumping involves moving the body ______ the ground. A. away from B. under C. inside
2. Which part of the body helps us to jump? A. Eyes B. Ears C. Feet and legs
3. Before jumping, pupils should ______. A. warm up B. push others C. run into people
4. Jumping on the spot means jumping and landing ______. A. in a different country B. in the same place C. on a chair
5. Which of these is a safe jumping practice? A. Pushing another pupil B. Jumping in a clear area C. Jumping on dangerous objects
6. When landing from a jump, pupils should land ______. A. on another pupil B. carelessly C. softly
7. Which of these can help pupils practise jumping? A. A safe rope on the ground B. A glass bottle C. A sharp object
8. Jumping can help to make the ______ stronger. A. legs B. ears C. hair
9. Pupils should keep enough ______ between one another when jumping. A. space B. noise C. food
10. What should a pupil do when feeling pain during jumping?. A. Push a friend. B. Continue jumping. C. Tell the teacher.
ANSWER KEY
1. A 2. C 3. A 4. B 5. B
6. C 7. A 8. A 9. A 10. C
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that jumping is the act of pushing the body off the ground with the feet and moving through the air before landing.
Pupils also learned how to perform simple jumps safely and that jumping helps to improve strength, balance, coordination and body control.
PRESENTATION
Step 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher asks pupils to stand and gently bend their knees. The teacher asks them to jump on the spot.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils stand, bend their knees and jump gently on the spot.
Step 2: Meaning of Jumping
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains the meaning of jumping and demonstrates how the legs and feet push the body off the ground.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen, observe and repeat the meaning of jumping.
Step 3: Types of Simple Jumps
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher demonstrates jumping on the spot, forward jumping and side jumping.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe and imitate the different simple jumps.
Step 4: Practical Demonstration
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher demonstrates how to bend the knees, swing the arms, push off the ground and land softly.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils practise the movements and land safely with their knees slightly bent.
Step 5: Importance of Jumping
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains that jumping helps to exercise the body, strengthen the legs, improve balance and develop coordination.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention some benefits of jumping.
Step 6: Safety Rules
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains safety rules such as warming up, keeping enough space, using a safe area and avoiding pushing others.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention and demonstrate safe behaviour during jumping activities.
Step 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides the pupils into four groups.
- Group 1: Practises jumping on the spot.
- Group 2: Practises simple forward jumps.
- Group 3: Practises simple side jumps.
- Group 4: Demonstrates safe landing after jumping.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its activities/work.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils work in groups, practise the activities and present their work.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews the meaning, types, practical activities, benefits and safety rules of jumping. The teacher asks pupils questions and observes their demonstrations.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer questions and demonstrate simple jumping activities safely.
CONCLUSION
The teacher reminds pupils that jumping is an important athletic activity. Pupils should practise jumping safely, follow instructions and give one another enough space.
NEXT LESSON
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What is jumping?
2. Mention two types of simple jumps.
3. Demonstrate how to jump and land safely.
4. Mention two benefits of jumping.
5. State two safety rules during jumping activities.

topics.title: Athletics: Long-Distance Races, Types of Long-Distance Races, Basic Activities in Long-Distance Races, and Safety Rules | Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 8 Physical and Health Education
topics.content:
PHYSICAL AND HEALTH EDUCATION (PHE)
PRIMARY 1 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 8
THEME - SPORTS AND GAMES
PREVIOUS LESSON - Athletics: Meaning of Athletics, Short-Distance Races, the 50-Metre Dash, and Health Benefits of Short-Distance Running | Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 6 Physical and Health Education
TOPIC - ATHLETICS: LONG DISTANCE RACES
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Types of Long-Distance Races
3. Basic Activities in Long-Distance Races
4. Safety Rules in Long-Distance Races
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of a long-distance race.
2. Mention examples of long-distance races.
3. Identify basic activities involved in long-distance races.
4. Demonstrate simple long-distance running activities.
5. State safety rules for long-distance races.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils can walk, run, jump and follow simple instructions during physical activities.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Pictures or charts of long-distance runners.
2. Whistle.
3. Cones or markers.
4. Measuring tape.
5. Open playground or running space.
METHODS OF TEACHING
The teacher uses observation, demonstration, questioning, identification, imitation, repetition, discussion and simple practical activities.
The teacher begins by asking pupils to walk and run slowly around the playground and explaining that some races require runners to run for a longer distance.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Physical and Health Education textbook for Primary 1.
2. Lagos State Scheme of Work for Physical and Health Education.
3. Teacher’s lesson guide.
4. Other relevant materials
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Athletics includes different activities such as running, jumping and throwing. Some running races are short, while others cover longer distances.
A long-distance race is a running race in which runners cover a long distance before reaching the finishing point.
Long-distance running requires patience, good breathing, body control and steady movement.
TYPES OF LONG DISTANCE RACES
Examples of long-distance races include:
- 800-metre race - runners cover 800 metres.
- 1,500-metre race - runners cover 1,500 metres.
- 5,000-metre race - runners cover 5,000 metres.
- 10,000-metre race - runners cover 10,000 metres.
For Primary 1 pupils, the teacher should use shorter, safe running distances for practical activities.
BASIC ACTIVITIES IN LONG-DISTANCE RACES
Basic activities include:
1. Walking and jogging: Pupils move slowly to prepare their bodies.
2. Warm-up exercises: Pupils stretch and move their bodies gently before running.
3. Steady running: Pupils run at a comfortable speed without rushing.
4. Running around markers: Pupils run around cones or other safe markers.
5. Stopping safely: Pupils slow down and stop when the teacher gives a signal.
6. Finishing the race: Pupils continue running until they reach the finishing point.
SIMPLE PRACTICAL DEMONSTRATION
The teacher demonstrates how to:
1. Stand properly at the starting point.
2. Start running when the teacher gives the signal.
3. Run at a steady and comfortable speed.
4. Keep a safe distance from other runners.
5. Follow the marked running path.
6. Slow down before stopping.
7. Stop safely at the finishing point.
8. Pupils practise the activities under the teacher’s supervision.
SAFETY RULES IN LONG-DISTANCE RACES
Pupils should:
1. Listen to the teacher’s instructions.
2. Warm up before running.
3. Run only in a safe and clear area.
4. Keep enough space between runners.
5. Avoid pushing or hitting other runners.
6. Wear suitable clothing and footwear.
7. Run at a safe speed.
8. Drink water when necessary.
9. Stop when the teacher gives the signal.
10. Tell the teacher if they feel pain or become unwell.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
Multiple Choice Questions
1. A long-distance race involves running over a ______ distance. A. long B. very short C. tiny
2. Which of these is a long-distance race? A. 10 B. 20 metres C. 5,000 metres
3. Before running, pupils should ______. A. sleep B. warm up C. push others
4. During a race, pupils should run at a ______ speed. A. safe B. dangerous C. careless
5. Which of these is a safety rule? A. Push other runners. B. Run into people. C. Listen to the teacher.
6. What should pupils do when the teacher gives the starting signal? A. Start the activity. B. Sit down. C. Push a friend.
7. Pupils should keep enough ______ between runners. A. noise B. space C. food
8. Which equipment can be used to mark a running path? A. Spoon B. Plate C. Cone
9. What should a pupil do when feeling pain during the activity? A. Continue without telling anyone. B. Tell the teacher. C. Push another pupil.
10. At the end of the race, pupils should ______ safely. A. stop B. fight C. push others
ANSWER KEY
1. A 2. C 3. B 4. A 5. C
6. A 7. B 8. C 9. B 10. A
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that a long-distance race is a running race in which runners cover a long distance. Examples include 800 metres, 1,500 metres, 5,000 metres and 10,000 metres.
Pupils also learned that they should warm up, run steadily, keep enough space and follow safety rules during long-distance activities.
PRESENTATION
Step 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher asks pupils to mention activities they do when playing outside. The teacher introduces long-distance running.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention activities such as walking, running and jumping.
Step 2: Meaning of Long-Distance Races
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains that a long-distance race is a race in which runners cover a long distance.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and repeat the meaning of long-distance race.
Step 3: Types of Long-Distance Races
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher shows pictures and mentions examples such as 800 metres, 1,500 metres, 5,000 metres and 10,000 metres.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify and mention the examples of long-distance races.
Step 4: Basic Activities
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher demonstrates walking, jogging, warming up, steady running and stopping safely.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils imitate the teacher and practise the activities.
Step 5: Safety Rules
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains safety rules such as keeping enough space, not pushing others, listening to instructions and running in a safe area.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention and demonstrate safe behaviours during running activities.
Step 6: Practical Running Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher marks a short and safe running path with cones. The teacher gives instructions and supervises pupils as they run steadily.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils run along the marked path, keep a safe distance and stop when instructed.
Step 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides the pupils into four groups.
- Group 1: Practises walking and jogging.
- Group 2: Practises simple warm-up exercises.
- Group 3: Practises steady running around markers.
- Group 4: Demonstrates safe stopping and finishing.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its activities/work.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils work in groups, practise the activities and present their work.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews the meaning, types, basic activities and safety rules of long-distance races. The teacher asks pupils simple questions and observes their practical demonstrations.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer questions and demonstrate simple running activities safely.
CONCLUSION
The teacher reminds pupils that long-distance races involve running over longer distances. Pupils should practise safely, follow instructions and keep enough space from one another.
NEXT LESSON
Athletics (Jumping): Meaning and Practical Demonstration of Jumping | Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 9 Physical and Health Education
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What is a long-distance race?
2. Mention two types of long-distance races.
3. Demonstrate how to run at a steady speed.
4. Mention two activities done during long-distance races.
5. State two safety rules for long-distance races.

topics.title: Athletics: Meaning of Athletics, Short-Distance Races, the 50-Metre Dash, and Health Benefits of Short-Distance Running | Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 6 Physical and Health Education
topics.content:
PHYSICAL AND HEALTH EDUCATION (PHE)
PRIMARY 1 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 6
THEME - SPORTS AND GAMES
PREVIOUS LESSON - Movement: Safety Rules in Basic Movements on the Playground Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 5 Physical and Health Education
TOPIC - ATHLETICS: SHORT DISTANCE RACES
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning of Athletics
3. Short-Distance Races and The 50-Metre Dash
4. Health Benefits of Short-Distance Running
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of athletics.
2. Identify short-distance races.
3. Explain the meaning of the 50-metre dash.
4. Demonstrate simple short-distance running.
5. Mention some health benefits of short-distance running.
6. Follow safety rules during running activities.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils can demonstrate simple movements such as walking, running, jumping, throwing, kicking, catching and stopping safely.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Athletics or running charts or pictures
2. Whistle
3. Measuring tape
4. Cones or markers
5. Open playground or running space
METHODS OF TEACHING
The teacher uses observation, demonstration, questioning, identification, discussion, imitation, repetition and simple practical activities.
The teacher begins by asking pupils if they have seen people running in a race and allowing them to demonstrate simple running movements.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Lagos State Scheme of Work
2. Physical and Health Education textbook for Primary 1
3. Teacher’s Guide
4. Relevant athletics charts and pictures
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
People take part in different sports and games to exercise their bodies and have fun. Athletics is one of the sports that involves activities such as running, jumping and throwing.
Running is an important athletics activity. Some races are short and require runners to run over a short distance.
MEANING OF ATHLETICS
Athletics is a group of sports that includes running, jumping and throwing activities.
Examples of athletics activities include:
- Short-distance races
- Long-distance races
- Jumping
- Throwing
SHORT-DISTANCE RACES
Short-distance races are races in which runners run over a short distance.
Examples include:
- 50-metre race
- 100-metre race
- 200-metre race
The 50-metre race is suitable for simple running practice for young pupils.
THE 50-METRE DASH
A 50-metre dash is a short-distance race in which pupils run over a distance of 50 metres from the starting point to the finishing point.
Simple Steps in the 50-Metre Dash
Pupils should:
1. Stand behind the starting line.
2. Listen carefully to the teacher.
3. Get ready when the teacher gives the instruction.
4. Start running when the teacher gives the signal.
5. Run straight towards the finishing line.
6. Slow down after crossing the finishing line.
7. Stop safely.
The teacher should ensure that pupils have enough space and that the running area is safe.
PRACTICAL DEMONSTRATION OF SHORT-DISTANCE RUNNING
The teacher marks a safe running area and demonstrates how to:
1. Stand behind the starting line.
2. Bend slightly and get ready.
3. Look forward.
4. Run straight ahead.
5. Move the arms gently while running.
6. Keep a safe distance from other pupils.
7. Cross the finishing line.
8. Slow down and stop safely.
Pupils practise short-distance running under the teacher’s supervision.
HEALTH BENEFITS OF SHORT-DISTANCE RUNNING
Short-distance running:
1. Exercises the body.
2. Keeps the body active.
3. Helps to make the legs stronger.
4. Helps to strengthen the muscles.
5. Improves body coordination.
6. Helps pupils stay physically fit.
7. Provides fun and enjoyment.
SAFETY DURING RUNNING ACTIVITIES
Pupils should:
1. Run in a safe and open space.
2. Follow the teacher’s instructions.
3. Wear suitable clothing and footwear.
4. Look forward while running.
5. Avoid pushing other pupils.
6. Keep enough space between runners.
7. Do not cross another runner’s lane.
8. Slow down after crossing the finishing line.
9. Stop when the teacher gives the instruction.
10. Tell the teacher if they feel pain or get injured.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
Multiple Choice Questions
1. What is athletics? A. Eating food B. Sleeping in class C. A group of sports involving running, jumping and throwing
2. Which of these is an athletics activity? A. Sleeping B. Running C. Reading
3. A short-distance race is a race over a ______ distance. A. short B. very long C. unknown
4. Which of these is a short-distance race? A. Eating race B. Swimming race C. 50-metre race
5. How long is the 50-metre dash? A. 20 metres B. 50 metres C. 100 metres
6. Before a race begins, pupils should stand behind the ______ line. A. classroom B. finishing C. starting
7. During a race, pupils should run ______. A. into others B. straight ahead C. backwards
8. Short-distance running helps to keep the body ______. A. active B. dirty C. weak
9. Pupils should wear suitable ______ when running. A. clothing and footwear B. books and bags C. jewellery
10. After crossing the finishing line, pupils should ______. A. run into other B. push others C. slow down safely
ANSWER KEY
1. C 2. B 3. A 4. C 5. B
6. C 7. B 8. A 9. A 10. C
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that athletics is a group of sports that includes running, jumping and throwing. They also learned that short-distance races are races over short distances, such as the 50-metre dash.
Pupils also learned that short-distance running exercises the body, strengthens the muscles and helps to keep the body active and fit. They should follow safety rules when running.
PRESENTATION
Step 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher asks pupils if they have seen people running in a race and allows them to demonstrate simple running movements.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils talk about running races and demonstrate simple running movements.
Step 2: Meaning of Athletics
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains the meaning of athletics and mentions running, jumping and throwing as examples.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and mention examples of athletics activities.
Step 3: Short-Distance Races
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains short-distance races and mentions the 50-metre, 100-metre and 200-metre races.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and identify short-distance races.
Step 4: The 50-Metre Dash
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains the 50-metre dash and marks the starting and finishing points.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the marked running area and identify the starting and finishing points.
Step 5: Demonstration of the 50-Metre Dash
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher demonstrates standing behind the starting line, running straight and slowing down after crossing the finishing line.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils practise running the short distance safely.
Step 6: Health Benefits and Safety
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains the health benefits of running and reviews safety rules such as not pushing others and keeping enough space.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention benefits of running and repeat the safety rules.
Step 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Demonstrate how to get ready for a race.
- Group 2: Demonstrate safe running.
- Group 3: Demonstrate how to start and finish a 50-metre race.
- Group 4: Mention and demonstrate three safety rules during running.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its activities.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils work in groups, practise the activities and present their work.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews athletics, short-distance races and the 50-metre dash and asks pupils simple questions.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and demonstrate simple running activities.
CONCLUSION
Athletics includes running, jumping and throwing activities. The 50-metre dash is a short-distance race. Running helps to exercise the body and keep it active. Pupils should always follow safety rules during running activities.
NEXT LESSON
Athletics: Long-Distance Races, Types of Long-Distance Races, Basic Activities in Long-Distance Races, and Safety Rules | Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 8 Physical and Health Education
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What is athletics?
2. Mention two short-distance races.
3. What is a 50-metre dash?
4. Demonstrate how to run safely in a short-distance race.
5. State two health benefits of short-distance running.

topics.title: Movement: Safety Rules in Basic Movements on the Playground Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 5 Physical and Health Education
topics.content:
PHYSICAL AND HEALTH EDUCATION (PHE)
PRIMARY 1 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 5
THEME - BASIC MOVEMENTS
PREVIOUS LESSON - Movement (Catching and Striking): Meaning and Practical Demonstration of Catching and Striking of Objects | Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 4 Physical and Health Education
TOPIC - SAFETY RULES IN BASIC MOVEMENTS
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning of Safety Rules
3. Safety Rules on the Playground
4. Practical Demonstration of Safety Rules During Basic Movements
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of safety rules.
2. Identify safety rules on the playground.
3. Mention some dangers that can occur when safety rules are not followed.
4. Demonstrate safe behaviour during basic movement activities.
5. Follow simple safety rules on the playground.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils can demonstrate simple movements such as walking, running, jumping, throwing, kicking, catching and striking.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Safety-rule charts or pictures
2. Whistle
3. Playground or open space
4. Soft balls
METHODS OF TEACHING
The teacher uses observation, demonstration, questioning, identification, discussion, imitation, repetition and simple practical activities.
The teacher begins by asking pupils to identify safe and unsafe behaviours they have seen on the playground.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Lagos State Scheme of Work
2. Physical and Health Education textbook for Primary 1
3. Teacher’s Guide
4. Relevant safety charts and pictures
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
The playground is a place where pupils can play and take part in movement activities. Pupils can walk, run, jump, throw, kick, catch and strike objects on the playground.
We need to follow safety rules to prevent injuries and keep everyone safe.
MEANING OF SAFETY RULES
Safety rules are simple instructions that help us avoid danger, accidents and injuries.
Safety rules help pupils to play and perform movement activities safely.
SAFETY RULES ON THE PLAYGROUND
Pupils should:
1. Listen to the teacher’s instructions.
2. Use a clean and safe playground.
3. Keep enough space between one another.
4. Avoid pushing other pupils.
5. Avoid running into other pupils.
6. Do not throw objects at other pupils.
7. Kick balls gently and carefully.
8. Use safe and suitable equipment.
9. Wear suitable clothing and footwear.
10. Avoid playing near dangerous objects.
11. Stop when the teacher blows the whistle.
12. Tell the teacher when they are injured or feel pain.
DANGERS OF NOT FOLLOWING SAFETY RULES
When pupils do not follow safety rules, they may:
1. Fall down.
2. Hurt themselves.
3. Hurt other pupils.
4. Collide with other pupils.
5. Damage equipment.
6. Have an accident.
PRACTICAL DEMONSTRATION OF SAFETY RULES
The teacher demonstrates safe and unsafe behaviours.
1. Safe Behaviours
Pupils can:
- Walk carefully.
- Run in the correct direction.
- Keep enough space.
- Throw and kick balls carefully.
- Follow instructions.
- Stop when the whistle is blown.
2. Unsafe Behaviours
Pupils should not:
- Push other pupils.
- Run into other pupils.
- Throw objects at people.
- Kick other pupils.
- Play near dangerous objects.
- Ignore the teacher’s instructions.
SIMPLE PLAYGROUND SAFETY ACTIVITIES
The teacher gives simple instructions for pupils to follow:
1. Stand in your position.
2. Leave enough space between yourself and others.
3. Walk forward carefully.
4. Run slowly when instructed.
5. Stop when the teacher blows the whistle.
6. Pick up equipment carefully.
7. Return equipment after use.
8. Report any injury to the teacher.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
Multiple Choice Questions
1. What are safety rules?
A. Rules that help us stay safe
B. Rules for sleeping
C. Rules for eating
2. We should ______ the teacher’s instructions. A. ignore B. follow C. hide from
3. On the playground, pupils should not ______ others. A. greet B. help C. push
4. We should keep enough ______ between one another. A. space B. noise C. food
5. What should pupils do when the whistle is blown? A. Run away B. Stop C. Push others
6. Which of these is safe on the playground?
A. Throwing a ball at someone’s face
B. Pushing a friend
C. Walking carefully
7. Pupils should wear suitable ______ during movement activities.
A. clothing and footwear
B. jewellery
C. school bags
8. If a pupil gets injured, the pupil should ______.
A. hide it
B. tell the teacher
C. continue playing
9. We should use ______ equipment for movement activities. A. broken B. dangerous C. safe
10. Following safety rules helps to prevent ______. A. accidents B. friendship C. learning
ANSWER KEY
1. A 2. B 3. C 4. A 5. B
2. C 7. A 8. B 9. C 10. A
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that safety rules are instructions that help us avoid danger and injuries during movement activities.
Pupils also learned that they should follow the teacher’s instructions, keep enough space, avoid pushing and report injuries. They should always behave safely on the playground.
PRESENTATION
Step 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher asks pupils to mention some activities they do on the playground.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention activities such as walking, running, jumping, throwing and kicking.
Step 2: Meaning of Safety Rules
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains the meaning of safety rules and gives simple examples.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and mention simple safety rules they know.
Step 3: Identifying Safe Behaviours
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher shows pictures of safe playground behaviours and asks pupils to identify them.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify and describe the safe behaviours.
Step 4: Identifying Unsafe Behaviours
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher shows pictures of unsafe behaviours such as pushing and running into others.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the unsafe behaviours and explain why they should be avoided.
Step 5: Practical Demonstration
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher demonstrates walking, running and stopping safely when the whistle is blown.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils imitate the movements and practise stopping safely.
Step 6: Safety Rules
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews rules such as keeping enough space, not pushing others and following instructions.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils repeat the safety rules and demonstrate them.
Step 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Demonstrate three safe playground behaviours.
- Group 2: Demonstrate three unsafe playground behaviours.
- Group 3: Demonstrate how to move safely while walking, running and stopping.
- Group 4: Mention and demonstrate three playground safety rules.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its activities.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils work in groups, practise the activities and present their work.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews the safety rules and asks pupils simple questions.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and demonstrate selected safety rules.
CONCLUSION
Safety rules help us stay safe during movement activities. Pupils should follow instructions, avoid pushing and running into others, use safe equipment and report injuries to the teacher.
NEXT LESSON
Athletics: Meaning of Athletics, Short-Distance Races, the 50-Metre Dash, and Health Benefits of Short-Distance Running | Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 6 Physical and Health Education
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What are safety rules?
2. Mention four safety rules on the playground.
3. Demonstrate two safe behaviours on the playground.
4. Mention two dangers of not following safety rules.
5. State two things you should do to stay safe during movement activities.

topics.title: Movement (Catching and Striking): Meaning and Practical Demonstration of Catching and Striking of Objects | Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 4 Physical and Health Education
topics.content:
PHYSICAL AND HEALTH EDUCATION (PHE)
PRIMARY 1 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 4
THEME - BASIC MOVEMENTS
PREVIOUS LESSON - Movement (Throwing and Kicking): Meaning and Practical Demonstration of Throwing and Kicking of Objects | Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 3 Physical and Health Education
TOPIC - CATCHING AND STRIKING OF OBJECTS
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning of Catching and Striking
3. Practical Demonstration of Catching and Striking of Objects
4. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
5. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of catching and striking.
2. Identify objects that can be caught and struck safely.
3. Demonstrate simple catching movements.
4. Demonstrate simple striking movements.
5. Follow simple safety rules during catching and striking activities.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils can identify common body parts and demonstrate simple movements such as throwing, kicking, walking, bending and stretching.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Soft balls
2. Balloons
3. Whistle
4. Open playground or classroom space
METHODS OF TEACHING
The teacher uses observation, demonstration, questioning, identification, imitation, repetition, discussion and simple practical activities.
The teacher begins by showing pupils a soft ball and a balloon and asking them to demonstrate how they can catch or gently strike an object safely.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Lagos State Scheme of Work
2. Physical and Health Education textbook for Primary 1
3. Teacher’s Guide
4. Relevant balls, charts and pictures
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
We use our hands and other body parts to perform different movements. We can catch objects that are moving towards us and strike objects gently using our hands or suitable equipment.
Catching and striking are simple movement skills used in games and physical activities.
MEANING OF CATCHING
Catching is the action of using the hands to receive and hold an object that is moving towards us.
Examples include:
- Catching a soft ball.
- Catching a balloon.
- Catching a bean bag.
MEANING OF STRIKING
Striking is the action of hitting an object gently with the hand or a suitable object.
Examples include:
- Hitting a balloon gently with the hand.
- Hitting a soft ball with the hand.
- Hitting a soft ball with a lightweight bat.
PRACTICAL DEMONSTRATION OF CATCHING AND STRIKING
1. Catching a Ball
Pupils can:
- Stand properly.
- Look at the ball.
- Stretch their hands forward.
- Keep their hands open.
- Receive the ball gently.
- Hold the ball with both hands.
2. Catching a Balloon
Pupils can:
- Watch the balloon carefully.
- Move their hands towards it.
- Catch it gently with both hands.
- Hold it carefully.
3. Striking a Balloon
Pupils can:
- Stand properly.
- Look at the balloon.
- Raise one hand.
- Hit the balloon gently.
- Watch the balloon move.
4. Striking a Soft Ball
The teacher demonstrates how to use the hand or a lightweight bat to strike a soft ball gently.
Pupils practise the movement under the teacher’s guidance.
SIMPLE CATCHING AND STRIKING ACTIVITIES
The teacher gives simple instructions for pupils to follow:
1. Stand properly.
2. Look at the ball.
3. Stretch your hands forward.
4. Catch the ball gently.
5. Hold the ball with both hands.
6. Raise your hand.
7. Strike the balloon gently.
8. Stop when the teacher says so.
IMPORTANCE OF CATCHING AND STRIKING
Catching and striking activities:
1. Exercise the body.
2. Keep the body active.
3. Make muscles stronger.
4. Help pupils control their body.
5. Help pupils develop coordination.
6. Help pupils take part in games and sports.
SAFETY DURING CATCHING AND STRIKING ACTIVITIES
Pupils should:
1. Use soft balls and safe objects.
2. Exercise in a safe and open space.
3. Follow the teacher’s instructions.
4. Avoid throwing objects at other pupils.
5. Avoid striking other pupils.
6. Keep enough space between one another.
7. Strike objects gently.
8. Stop when the teacher says so.
9. Tell the teacher if they feel pain or get injured.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
Multiple Choice Questions
1. What is catching?
A. Receiving and holding an object with the hands
B. Sleeping
C. Running away
2. What is striking?
A. Drinking water
B. Hitting an object gently
C. Sitting down
3. Which of these can be caught safely?
A. A sharp stone
B. A soft ball
C. A broken bottle
4. Which body part can we use to catch a ball? A. Hand B. Ear C. Nose
5. What should we do when catching a ball?
A. Run away
B. Look at the ball
C. Close our eyes
6. Which of these is suitable for catching practice?
A. Sharp stone
B. Glass cup
C. Soft ball
7. We should strike an object ______.
A. very dangerously
B. at a person
C. gently
8. During catching and striking, pupils should keep enough ______. A. noise B. space C. water
9. Catching and striking help to keep the body ______. A. active B. dirty C. weak
10. When the teacher says stop, pupils should ______.
A. continue playing
B. run into others
C. stop
ANSWER KEY
1. A 2. C 3. B 4. A 5. C
6. B 7. C 8. B 9. A 10. C
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that catching means receiving and holding an object with the hands. They also learned that striking means hitting an object gently with the hand or a suitable object.
Pupils also learned how to catch and strike objects safely. They should use soft objects, keep enough space, follow instructions and avoid striking other pupils.
PRESENTATION
Step 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher shows pupils a soft ball and a balloon and asks them what they can do with them.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the objects and mention what they can do with them.
Step 2: Meaning of Catching
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains the meaning of catching and demonstrates how to catch a soft ball with both hands.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe and imitate the teacher’s catching movement.
Step 3: Meaning of Striking
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains the meaning of striking and demonstrates how to strike a balloon gently with the hand.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe and imitate the striking movement.
Step 4: Demonstration of Catching
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher demonstrates watching a soft ball, stretching out the hands and catching it gently.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils practise catching the ball with both hands.
Step 5: Demonstration of Striking
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher demonstrates striking a balloon gently with the hand and striking a soft ball with a lightweight bat.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils practise striking the objects carefully.
Step 6: Safety Rules
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains safety rules such as using soft objects, keeping enough space and not striking other pupils.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen, repeat the safety rules and demonstrate safe behaviour.
Step 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Demonstrate three simple catching activities.
- Group 2: Demonstrate three simple striking activities.
- Group 3: Demonstrate catching a soft ball with both hands.
- Group 4: Demonstrate three safety rules during catching and striking activities.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its activities.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils work in groups, practise the activities and present their activities.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews the meaning of catching and striking and asks pupils simple questions.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and demonstrate selected catching and striking movements.
CONCLUSION
Catching means receiving and holding an object with the hands, while striking means hitting an object gently. Pupils should practise these skills carefully and always follow safety rules.
NEXT LESSON
Movement: Safety Rules in Basic Movements on the Playground Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 5 Physical and Health Education
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What is catching?
2. What is striking?
3. Differentiate between catching and striking.
4. Demonstrate two ways of catching an object.
5. Demonstrate two ways of striking an object.
6. State two safety rules during catching and striking activities.

topics.title: Movement (Throwing and Kicking): Meaning and Practical Demonstration of Throwing and Kicking of Objects | Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 3 Physical and Health Education
topics.content:
PHYSICAL AND HEALTH EDUCATION (PHE)
PRIMARY 1 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 3
THEME - BASIC MOVEMENTS
PREVIOUS LESSON - Movement: Practical Demonstration of Moving Our Body Parts Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 2 Physical and Health Education
TOPIC - THROWING AND KICKING OF OBJECTS
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning of Throwing and Kicking
3. Practical Demonstration of Throwing and Kicking
4. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
5. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of throwing and kicking.
2. Identify objects that can be thrown and kicked safely.
3. Demonstrate simple throwing movements.
4. Demonstrate simple kicking movements.
5. Follow safety rules during throwing and kicking activities.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils can identify common body parts and demonstrate simple movements such as raising, bending, stretching, walking and jumping.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Soft balls
2. Bean bags
3. Whistle
4. Open playground or classroom space
METHODS OF TEACHING
The teacher uses observation, demonstration, questioning, identification, imitation, repetition, discussion and simple practical activities.
The teacher begins by showing pupils a soft ball and a bean bag and asking them to demonstrate how they can throw or kick an object safely.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Lagos State Scheme of Work
2. Physical and Health Education textbook for Primary 1
3. Teacher’s Guide
4. Relevant balls, charts and pictures
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
We use different parts of our body to move objects. We can use our hands to throw an object and our feet to kick an object.
Throwing and kicking are important movement skills used in games and other physical activities.
MEANING OF THROWING
Throwing is the action of using the hand or arm to send an object away from the body.
Examples of objects that can be thrown safely include:
- Soft balls
- Bean bags
- Small soft objects
These include:
- Throwing a soft ball to a friend.
- Throwing a bean bag into a basket.
- Throwing a ball towards a target.
We can throw an object forward, upward or towards a safe target.
MEANING OF KICKING
Kicking is the action of using the foot to hit or move an object.
A soft ball can be kicked forward or towards a safe target.
Examples include:
- Kicking a football.
- Kicking a soft ball towards a target.
- Kicking a ball to a friend.
Kicking is commonly used when playing games such as football.
PRACTICAL DEMONSTRATION OF THROWING AND KICKING
1. Throwing a Ball
Pupils can:
- Stand properly.
- Hold the soft ball with one or both hands.
- Look towards the direction of the target.
- Raise the hand gently.
- Throw the ball forward.
- Throw the ball towards a safe target.
2. Throwing a Bean Bag
Pupils can:
- Hold the bean bag firmly.
- Stand facing the target.
- Look at the target.
- Move the hand forward.
- Release the bean bag gently.
- Watch where the bean bag lands.
3. Kicking a Ball
Pupils can:
- Stand behind the ball.
- Look at the direction of the target.
- Place one foot beside the ball.
- Use the other foot to kick the ball gently.
- Kick the ball forward.
- Kick the ball towards a safe target.
4. Throwing and Kicking to a Partner
The teacher pairs pupils and allows them to practise simple throwing and kicking activities.
Pupils should throw the soft ball gently to a partner and kick the ball gently towards a partner.
SIMPLE THROWING AND KICKING ACTIVITIES
The teacher gives simple instructions for pupils to follow:
1. Hold the ball.
2. Look at the target.
3. Throw the ball forward.
4. Pick up the ball carefully.
5. Stand behind the ball.
6. Kick the ball gently.
7. Walk back to your position.
8. Stand still.
IMPORTANCE OF THROWING AND KICKING
Throwing and kicking activities:
1. Exercise the body.
2. Keep the body active.
3. Make muscles stronger.
4. Help us develop body control.
5. Help us develop coordination.
6. Help us take part in games and sports.
SAFETY DURING THROWING AND KICKING ACTIVITIES
Pupils should:
1. Use soft balls and safe objects.
2. Exercise in a safe and open space.
3. Follow the teacher’s instructions.
4. Avoid throwing objects at other pupils.
5. Avoid kicking other pupils.
6. Keep enough space between one another.
7. Move gently.
8. Stop when the teacher says so.
9. Tell the teacher if they feel pain or get injured.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
Multiple Choice Questions
1. What is throwing?
A. Sitting
B. Sleeping
C. Sending an object away with the hand
2. What is kicking?
A. Clapping the hands
B. Hitting or moving an object with the foot
C. Raising the head
3. Which of these can be thrown safely? A. A stone B. A sharp object C. A soft ball
4. Which body part do we mainly use for kicking? A. Foot B. Ear C. Nose
5. Before throwing a ball, we should look at the ______. A. floor B. target C. ceiling
6. Which of these is suitable for throwing practice? A. Stone  B. Glass cup C. Soft ball
7. We should not throw objects at other pupils’ ______. A. faces B. shoes C. bags
8. During kicking practice, pupils should kick the ball ______. A. very hard B. gently C. at other pupils
9. Throwing and kicking can help to keep the body ______. A. active B. dirty C. weak
10. When the teacher says stop, pupils should ______.
A. continue kicking
B. run into others
C. stop moving
ANSWER KEY
1. C 2. B 3. C 4. A 5. B
6. B 7. A 8. B 9. A 10. C
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that throwing means using the hand or arm to send an object away from the body. They also learned that kicking means using the foot to hit or move an object.
Pupils also learned how to throw and kick soft objects safely. They should follow instructions, keep enough space and avoid throwing or kicking objects at other pupils.
PRESENTATION
Step 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher shows pupils a soft ball and asks them what they can do with it.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the ball and mention things they can do with it.
Step 2: Meaning of Throwing
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains the meaning of throwing and demonstrates how to throw a soft ball forward.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and imitate the teacher’s throwing movement.
Step 3: Meaning of Kicking
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains the meaning of kicking and demonstrates how to kick a soft ball gently.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe and imitate the kicking movement.
Step 4: Demonstration of Throwing
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher demonstrates holding a ball, looking at a target and throwing the ball gently towards it.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils practise throwing the ball towards a safe target.
Step 5: Demonstration of Kicking
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher demonstrates standing behind a ball and kicking it gently towards a target.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils practise kicking the ball carefully.
Step 6: Safety Rules
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains safety rules such as using soft objects, keeping enough space and avoiding throwing or kicking at other pupils.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen, repeat the safety rules and demonstrate safe behaviour.
Step 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Demonstrate three simple throwing activities.
- Group 2: Demonstrate three simple kicking activities.
- Group 3: Demonstrate throwing a soft ball towards a target.
- Group 4: Demonstrate three safety rules during throwing and kicking activities.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its activities.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils work in groups, practise the activities and present their activities.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews the meaning of throwing and kicking and asks pupils simple questions.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and demonstrate selected throwing and kicking movements.
CONCLUSION
Throwing and kicking are simple movement skills. We can throw objects with our hands and kick objects with our feet. We should always follow instructions and perform these activities safely.
NEXT LESSON
Movement (Catching and Striking): Meaning and Practical Demonstration of Catching and Striking of Objects | Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 4 Physical and Health Education
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What is throwing?
2. What is kicking?
3. Differentiate between throwing and kicking.
4. Demonstrate two ways of throwing an object.
5. Demonstrate two ways of kicking an object.
6. State two safety rules during throwing and kicking activities.

topics.title: Movement: Moving Our Body Parts | Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 1 Physical and Health Education
topics.content:
PHYSICAL AND HEALTH EDUCATION (PHE)
PRIMARY 1 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 1
THEME - BASIC MOVEMENTS
PREVIOUS LESSON -
TOPIC - MOVING OUR BODY PARTS
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning of movement
3. Body parts that can move and Ways of moving our body parts
4. Simple body movements and Importance of body movement
5. Safety during movement activities
6. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
7. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain movement in simple words.
2. Identify body parts that can move.
3. Demonstrate simple movements of the body.
4. Mention some benefits of moving the body.
5. Follow simple safety rules during movement activities.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils can identify common body parts such as the head, hands, legs, arms and feet.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Pictures of body parts
2. Body-part charts
3. An open space for simple movement activities.
METHODS OF TEACHING
The teacher uses observation, demonstration, questioning, identification, imitation, repetition, discussion and simple practical activities.
The teacher begins by asking pupils to stand up and demonstrate simple movements such as raising their hands, bending their knees and moving their feet.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Lagos State Scheme of Work
2. Physical and Health Education textbook for Primary 1
3. Teacher’s Guide
4. Relevant charts and pictures
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Our body can move in different ways. We use our body parts to walk, run, jump, bend, stretch, clap and play.
Movement helps us to exercise our body and keep it active.
MEANING OF MOVEMENT
Movement means changing the position of the body or a body part.
For example, when we raise our hand, our hand moves from one position to another.
BODY PARTS THAT CAN MOVE
Many parts of our body can move.
Examples include:
- Head
- Neck
- Arms
- Hands
- Fingers
- Waist
- Legs
- Knees
- Feet
- Toes
WAYS OF MOVING OUR BODY PARTS
We can move our body parts in different ways.
1. Raising - We can raise our hands above our heads.
2. Bending - We can bend our knees, arms and body.
3. Stretching - We can stretch our arms and legs.
4. Clapping - We can move our hands together to clap.
5. Turning - We can turn our head or body gently.
6. Walking - We move our legs and feet when we walk.
7. Jumping - We use our legs and feet when we jump.
8. Running - We move our legs and arms when we run.
SIMPLE BODY MOVEMENTS
Pupils can practise these simple movements:
1. Raise both hands.
2. Lower both hands.
3. Bend the knees.
4. Stretch the arms.
5. Clap the hands.
6. Turn the head gently.
7. Walk forward.
8. Jump gently.
9. Run slowly in an open space.
IMPORTANCE OF MOVING OUR BODY
Moving our body:
1. Helps us exercise.
2. Keeps our body active.
3. Helps our muscles become stronger.
4. Helps us move from one place to another.
5. Helps us play and take part in activities.
6. Helps us develop body coordination.
SAFETY DURING MOVEMENT ACTIVITIES
We should be careful when doing movement activities.
1. Use a safe and open space.
2. Do not push other pupils.
3. Do not run into other pupils.
4. Follow the teacher’s instructions.
5. Wear suitable clothing and footwear.
6. Stop when the teacher says so.
7. Report any pain or injury to the teacher.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
Multiple Choice Questions
1. Movement means changing the ______ of the body or a body part. A. name B. colour C. position
2. Which body part can we use for clapping? A. Eyes B. Nose C. Hands
3. We use our ______ to walk. A. legs B. ears C. mouth
4. Which of these is a body movement? A. Jumping B. Sleeping C. Eating
5. We can move our hands by ______ them. A. hiding B. raising C. washing
6. Which body part helps us to bend when we walk or run? A. Knee B. Ear. C. Eye
7. Moving our body helps to keep us ______. A. dirty B. active C. sleepy
8. We should not ______ other pupils during movement activities. A. push B. greet C. help
9. We should do movement activities in a ______ place. A. crowded B. dangerous C. safe
10. When the teacher says stop, pupils should ______.
A. push others
B. run faster
C. stop moving
ANSWER KEY
1. C 2. C 3. A 4. B 5. A
6. A 7. B 8. A 9. B 10. C
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that movement means changing the position of the body or a body part. Parts such as the hands, arms, legs, knees, feet and head can move in different ways.
Pupils also learned that movement helps to exercise the body and keep it active. They should follow safety rules during movement activities.
PRESENTATION
Step 1: Introduction
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher asks pupils to stand and move their hands, legs and heads gently.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils follow the instructions and move their body parts.
Step 2: Meaning of Movement
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains the meaning of movement using simple examples.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen and repeat the meaning of movement.
Step 3: Body Parts That Can Move
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher points to different body parts and asks pupils to identify them.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify and name the body parts.
Step 4: Ways of Moving the Body
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher demonstrates raising, bending, stretching, clapping, walking and jumping.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils imitate the teacher’s movements.
Step 5: Importance of Movement
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains how movement helps exercise the body and keeps it active.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention some benefits of movement.
Step 6: Safety During Movement
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher explains simple safety rules for movement activities.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils demonstrate safe movement and state safety rules.
Step 7: Group Activity
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Demonstrate three movements of the hands.
- Group 2: Demonstrate three movements of the legs.
- Group 3: Demonstrate three simple whole-body movements.
- Group 4: Mention three safety rules during movement activities.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its work.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils work in groups, practise their movements and present their activities.
Step 8: Lesson Summary and Evaluation
Teacher’s Activities: The teacher reviews the meaning, types and importance of body movement and asks pupils simple questions.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and demonstrate some movements.
CONCLUSION
Our body can move in many ways. Moving our body helps us to exercise and stay active. We should always move safely and follow the teacher’s instructions.
NEXT LESSON
Movement: Practical Demonstration of Moving Our Body Parts Primary 1 (Basic 1) First Term Week 2 Physical and Health Education
LESSON EVALUATION
What is movement?
1. Mention four body parts that can move.
2. Mention three ways of moving the body.
3. State two importance of body movement.
4. Mention two safety rules during movement activities.
